raw_statement: By 31 December 2032, spending on security and resilience — cyber protection, fraud/scam defense, physical/home security, defense-adjacent and civil-preparedness goods — grows faster than discretionary convenience spending in high-income markets, operationalized as: (a) enterprise cybersecurity budgets treated as non-discretionary, growing >10% CAGR 2026–2032 even in years of flat overall IT spend; (b) a majority of surveyed adults in the US/EU report paying for at least one dedicated security/identity/fraud-protection subscription; and (c) at least five OECD states legislate mandatory resilience procurement (energy, cyber, or stockpiles).
title: Security as Standing Consumption: Resilience Spend Outgrowing Convenience Spend in High-Income Markets by 2032

formalized.statement: [thesis] By 31 December 2032, security and resilience spending — enterprise cyber, consumer fraud/identity protection, physical/home security, defense-adjacent and civil-preparedness goods — compounds faster than discretionary convenience spending in high-income markets. Resolution requires at least two of three sub-conditions: (a) [measurable] global enterprise cybersecurity spend grows >10% CAGR over FY2026–FY2032 with no calendar year below +7% y/y, including in any year where total enterprise IT spend grows <2% in nominal USD; (b) [measurable] in nationally representative surveys in the US and at least three EU member states, >50% of adults report currently paying (directly or as an explicitly priced bundle line) for at least one dedicated security, identity, fraud-protection, monitored-alarm or cyber-insurance subscription; (c) [measurable] at least five OECD member states have enacted binding legislation or statutory instruments mandating resilience procurement — strategic stockpiles, backup generation/firm-capacity obligations, or mandatory cybersecurity controls with procurement-linked enforcement — with effective dates on or before 2032.
formalized.population: Households and enterprises in high-income markets (OECD, primarily US, EU-27, UK, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia), plus the governments that procure on their behalf; secondarily the vendor universe supplying cyber, identity, physical security, backup power, defense and preparedness goods.
formalized.behavior: Reclassification of protection from an optional, event-driven purchase into a recurring, budgeted, often legally mandated line item — paid ahead of, and at the expense of, optimization/convenience/entertainment spend.
formalized.observable_outcome: Security/resilience categories grow their share of both enterprise IT budgets and household recurring subscription wallets, become embedded in statute, and show low cyclicality (spend maintained through a growth slowdown or nominal budget freeze), while convenience/discretionary categories (streaming, leisure subscriptions, non-essential upgrades) decelerate or lose share.
formalized.measurable_metric: (1) Enterprise cybersecurity spend CAGR 2026–2032 vs total IT spend CAGR (Gartner/IDC/Canalys reconciled, nominal USD) — target >10% vs gap of >600bps; (2) share of US/EU adults with ≥1 paid security/identity/fraud subscription (Pew, Eurobarometer, FCA/Ofcom, national statistics) — target >50%; (3) count of OECD jurisdictions with binding resilience-procurement statutes in force — target ≥5; (4) supporting: security/defense/resilience-linked revenue growth vs discretionary-consumer revenue growth across a matched listed universe; (5) elasticity test: cyber budget y/y growth in the worst IT-spend year of the window.the composite resolves TRUE if ≥2 of (a)(b)(c) hold.'

mechanism.human_motivation: [inference] Loss aversion dominates gain-seeking once threat becomes salient and personal. AI-generated scams, deepfake voice fraud, ransomware on hospitals and utilities, drone strikes on infrastructure, grid failures and war proximity convert an abstract tail risk into a vivid, recently-experienced one. People and boards do not optimize expected value; they buy the elimination of a dreaded, uncontrollable, high-variance outcome — and they keep paying because cancelling protection requires an explicit act of self-exposure.
mechanism.friction_removed: [inference] Historically resilience was expensive, technical and required behavioral discipline (patching, password hygiene, drills, generators, stockpiles). The friction removed is cognitive and operational: security is being packaged as a managed subscription, an insurance-like product, a bundled telco/bank/OEM line item, or an autonomous agent that acts without the user. The buyer no longer has to be competent — only willing to pay. [fact] Consumer-grade examples already shipping: bank-embedded scam detection, card-issuer identity monitoring, telco spam/scam call filtering, cloud-managed home cameras, managed detection and response (MDR) for SMEs.
mechanism.enabling_technology: [fact] AI on both sides of the ledger: generative models industrialize fraud (voice cloning, phishing at scale, synthetic identity) while the same models power behavioral detection, anomaly scoring, autonomous SOC triage and agentic response. [fact] Supporting stack: cloud-delivered SASE/zero-trust, identity infrastructure, edge/on-device inference for privacy-preserving detection, cheap IP cameras and sensors, behind-the-meter generation and storage, and digital identity/attestation schemes (eIDAS 2.0, mDL).
mechanism.economic_incentive: [inference] Expected loss avoided exceeds premium for the buyer; for the seller, security is the rare software category with negative price elasticity at the point of fear and high renewal rates. [fact] Insurance and regulation externalize the incentive: cyber insurers condition coverage on controls (MFA, EDR, backups), lenders and auditors condition terms on attestations, and liability regimes (EU NIS2, DORA, CRA, SEC disclosure rules) make non-spending a board-level personal risk. [inference] Once protection is a condition of transacting, it stops competing with convenience for wallet share and starts competing with rent.
mechanism.trust_requirement: [inference] The buyer must trust a vendor with the keys to the thing being protected — endpoints, identity, home video, financial credentials. This is the binding constraint: each vendor breach (SolarWinds, Okta, Change Healthcare, CrowdStrike's 2024 outage) is a trust shock that re-prices the category. Consolidation toward a few audited, insured, certified platforms is the likely resolution; certification regimes and government attestation act as trust substitutes.
mechanism.distribution_mechanism: [fact/inference] Three channels, in ascending order of penetration: (1) direct subscription (small, high-intent minority); (2) bundling into products people already buy — banks, card networks, telcos, ISPs, insurers, device OEMs, Amazon/Google home ecosystems — which is how consumer penetration crosses 50% without an explicit purchase decision; (3) statutory mandate and public procurement, which converts adoption into compliance. Enterprise distribution runs through MSPs/MSSPs, cyber insurers and cloud marketplaces.
mechanism.network_effects: [inference] Moderate and mostly data-side: threat intelligence, fraud graphs and device reputation improve with scale, giving incumbents a compounding detection advantage (a data network effect, not a social one). Negative externality version: as more entities harden, attackers concentrate on the unprotected, raising the private return to spending and producing a herding/ratchet dynamic. Standards and interoperability (SBOM, attestation, shared fraud signals between banks) add a coordination layer.
mechanism.switching_costs: [inference] High in enterprise (agent deployment, policy configuration, integration debt, audit continuity, multi-year ELAs, platform consolidation discounts) and moderate-to-high in consumer (identity histories, camera footage archives, bundled pricing, inertia on autorenewal). Regulation raises switching costs further by attaching certifications to specific implementations. This is why the category's revenue is durable even when growth decelerates.
mechanism.regulatory_constraints: [fact] Regulation is predominantly a tailwind here, not a constraint: NIS2, DORA, the EU Cyber Resilience Act, UK Online Safety/APP fraud reimbursement rules, SEC cyber disclosure, CMMC in US defense supply chains, EU/NATO defense-spending floors, energy reliability standards. [inference] Counter-forces exist: privacy law limits surveillance-based detection, antitrust/consumer-protection scrutiny of junk-fee-style bundled protection products, budget politics on stockpiles, and the risk that mandates cap prices or commoditize baseline protection into 'must be free' (as happened with antivirus and credit monitoring).

analogues.name: Post-9/11 homeland and aviation security buildout (TSA, DHS, screening capex)
analogues.mechanism: Salient catastrophic event converts protection from optional to mandatory; state legislates procurement and creates a permanent budget line that never reverts.
analogues.lesson: [fact] US homeland-security outlays roughly tripled within a decade and never returned to baseline. [inference] Ratchet effects in state security budgets are near-irreversible once institutionalized in an agency and a procurement statute — the legislative sub-condition (c) is the most durable of the three.

analogues.name: Sarbanes-Oxley compliance spending after Enron/WorldCom
analogues.mechanism: Trust failure → statutory mandate → non-discretionary recurring spend with personal liability attached to executives.
analogues.lesson: [fact] SOX created a multi-billion-dollar permanent audit/controls market within ~3 years. [inference] Personal officer liability is the single most powerful converter of discretionary spend into mandatory spend — SEC cyber-disclosure and NIS2 management liability replicate this exact design.

analogues.name: EMV chip-card migration and PCI-DSS after mass card fraud
analogues.mechanism: Liability shift plus industry standard forces universal upgrade; the payer is the merchant, the beneficiary is system-wide trust.
analogues.lesson: [fact] US EMV took ~11 years from EU rollout because the mandate was a private liability shift, not law. [inference] Where liability can be reassigned contractually, adoption is complete but slow; legislation compresses the timeline by ~3–5 years.

analogues.name: GDPR-driven privacy and data-governance spending
analogues.mechanism: Regulation with turnover-linked fines creates a new mandatory enterprise budget category from near zero.
analogues.lesson: [fact] A DPO/privacy-tech industry appeared within three years of enforcement date. [inference] Mandates create spend faster than fear does, but the spend is capped at the compliance floor — growth decays to GDP+ once the checkbox is met, which is the main risk to the >10% CAGR sub-condition.

analogues.name: Y2K remediation programs
analogues.mechanism: Salient, date-certain catastrophic risk drives emergency non-discretionary IT spend across every enterprise simultaneously.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Enormous spend surge followed by a sharp 2000–2002 air pocket. [inference] The clearest failure mode for this thesis: fear-funded spend with a defined terminal date mean-reverts violently. Durability requires a *recurring adversary*, which cyber and fraud have and Y2K did not.

analogues.name: Consumer antivirus subscriptions (Norton/McAfee era)
analogues.mechanism: Household purchase of protection against an invisible digital threat, sold as an annual subscription via OEM bundling.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Reached majority PC penetration largely through OEM bundling, then was commoditized to zero by Microsoft Defender being made free and good enough. [inference] Consumer sub-condition (b) is achievable via bundling but the *paid* qualifier is fragile: platform owners absorbing baseline security into the OS/bank/telco destroys the standalone price point while raising penetration.

analogues.name: Identity-theft protection and credit monitoring after mass breaches (LifeLock, Equifax 2017)
analogues.mechanism: Recurring personal-harm risk creates a consumer subscription category; breached firms distribute it free as remediation.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Category grew to billions in revenue but paid penetration stalled well below 50% in the US because free monitoring from card issuers, breach settlements and credit bureaus crowded out paid plans. [inference] Direct evidence that sub-condition (b) at >50% *paid* is the hardest of the three — it likely requires the survey to count bundled bank/telco/insurer protection lines.

analogues.name: Home alarm monitoring adoption (ADT and successors, US)
analogues.mechanism: Physical threat salience plus recurring monitoring fee; crime-rate-driven, insurance-discount-supported.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Peaked around ~20–25% of US households despite decades of marketing and insurance discounts. [inference] Fear alone does not produce majority household penetration when install friction and monthly cost are high — the frictionless, hardware-light version is what crosses 50%.

analogues.name: Video doorbells and DIY home cameras (Ring, Nest, Wyze)
analogues.mechanism: Same protective motivation, but friction collapsed: no installer, no contract, cheap hardware, cloud subscription attached afterwards.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Went from niche to tens of millions of US households in under a decade, with attach-rate cloud subscriptions. [inference] This is the template for sub-condition (b): protection sold as a cheap device plus a small recurring fee, distributed by a platform, adopted by a majority within ~7 years. Friction removal, not threat level, was the swing variable.

analogues.name: European defense spending reversal after Russia's invasion of Ukraine
analogues.mechanism: Geopolitical shock converts a 30-year declining budget line into a legislated floor with multi-year procurement commitments.
analogues.lesson: [fact] NATO members moved from chronic 2%-target undershoot to legislated increases and multi-decade procurement programs within 2–3 years. [inference] Strongest live evidence for sub-condition (c): state resilience spend re-rates fast and is politically ratcheted, though delivery lags funding by 3–5 years.

analogues.name: Cold War civil defense and household fallout shelters
analogues.mechanism: Maximal threat salience plus state encouragement of household preparedness purchases.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Despite peak fear and federal promotion, private shelter construction reached only low single-digit percentages of US households. [inference] Households refuse resilience purchases that demand large capex, effort and confrontation with the threat; the pattern only works when protection is cheap, passive and recurring. This is the base-rate counterweight to the household leg of the thesis.

analogues.name: Post-COVID pandemic preparedness stockpiles and PPE capacity
analogues.mechanism: Catastrophic event triggers state and corporate stockpiling mandates and domestic capacity subsidies.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Enormous immediate procurement surge; by 2023–24 many national stockpile programs were quietly defunded and domestic PPE producers failed. [inference] Resilience mandates without a permanent statutory funding mechanism decay within ~3 years of the salient event — sub-condition (c) should be scored on *binding statutes with enforcement*, not announcements.

analogues.name: NERC CIP critical-infrastructure standards after the 2003 Northeast blackout
analogues.mechanism: Infrastructure failure → mandatory, auditable reliability and cyber standards with financial penalties for utilities.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Created a permanent, penalty-enforced compliance spend category across North American utilities. [inference] Energy-sector resilience mandates are the most likely of the five OECD statutes to materialize, because the regulator, the asset owner and the ratepayer recovery mechanism already exist.

analogues.name: Backup generation and home standby power after Texas Uri / California PSPS / European energy crisis
analogues.mechanism: Reliability of a public utility ceases to be assumed; households and enterprises buy private firm capacity.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Standby generator and home-battery attach rates rose sharply in outage-exposed regions, and hyperscalers now contract private generation directly. [inference] Resilience spend concentrates geographically around experienced failures — national averages understate the behavior change; the thesis should be measured regionally as well as nationally.

analogues.name: Cyber insurance market formation and control mandates post-ransomware wave
analogues.mechanism: Insurers price and then *mandate* security controls as a condition of coverage, converting best practice into procurement requirement.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Premiums spiked, then insurers made MFA, EDR and immutable backups underwriting prerequisites, pulling forward billions of tooling spend. [inference] Private liability transfer is a faster mandate channel than legislation and should be tracked as a leading indicator for sub-condition (a).

analogues.name: AML/KYC compliance spending after the USA PATRIOT Act and FATF expansion
analogues.mechanism: Statutory obligation with criminal liability makes financial-crime prevention a permanently growing, headcount-heavy cost centre.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Global AML compliance spend grew for two decades at rates far above bank IT spend and proved fully insensitive to the credit cycle. [inference] This is the closest structural precedent for the 'non-discretionary even in a flat-budget year' claim in sub-condition (a): mandated crime-prevention spend is counter-cyclical to the budget, not pro-cyclical.

analogues.name: Automotive safety mandates (seatbelts, airbags, ABS, ADAS)
analogues.mechanism: Safety features migrate from expensive option → marketing differentiator → legal requirement → invisible standard cost.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Each wave followed the same option→mandate path over 10–20 years and permanently raised unit content value. [inference] Terminal state of a successful security thesis is *embedded and mandatory*, which raises supplier volumes but transfers pricing power to the OEM/platform — good for content growth, bad for standalone vendor margins.

analogues.name: Fire insurance and municipal fire codes after the great urban fires (London 1666, Chicago 1871)
analogues.mechanism: Catastrophe → private protection market → building codes and mandatory insurance → permanent infrastructure category.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Protection evolved from a private subscription (fire marks) into universal, code-mandated, insurer-enforced infrastructure. [inference] The longest-duration version of this mechanism: security categories that survive become invisible infrastructure with utility-like economics and regulated returns rather than high-growth software multiples.

analogues.name: Bank deposit insurance and bank examination regime (FDIC, 1933–)
analogues.mechanism: Systemic trust collapse → state-mandated, industry-funded protection scheme that becomes permanent, unquestioned infrastructure.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Became universal within a few years and has never been repealed. [inference] Where protection is a public good with free-rider problems, the state — not the household — becomes the buyer; the investable exposure then sits with suppliers and compliance vendors, not consumer subscription franchises.

analogues.name: Water filtration and bottled water after contamination scares (Flint, Cryptosporidium, PFAS)
analogues.mechanism: Loss of trust in a public utility drives private, recurring household protection purchases.
analogues.lesson: [fact] Household water filtration crossed a majority of US homes in under two decades once the product became cheap and passive. [inference] Loss of confidence in a public guarantee reliably creates a mass-market private protection category — the analogue for 'fraud protection' if trust in banks/telcos to stop scams erodes further.

reference_class.description: [definition] The reference class is 'threat-salience-driven reclassification of protection from discretionary to non-discretionary spend', split into three sub-classes matching the three resolution conditions. Sub-class A (enterprise mandated-protection budgets): SOX, GDPR, AML/KYC, PCI-DSS/EMV, NERC CIP, cyber insurance control mandates, Y2K — 7 cases, 7 produced a durable multi-year spend category, but 2 (Y2K, GDPR) decayed to low-growth within ~5 years of the compliance floor being met, and only those with a *recurring adaptive adversary* (AML, PCI, cyber insurance) sustained double-digit growth for a decade-plus. Sub-class B (household paid protection subscriptions): antivirus, identity/credit monitoring, monitored alarms, video doorbells, water filtration, fallout shelters — 6 cases, 4 reached majority or near-majority penetration, 2 stalled badly (alarms ~25%, shelters <5%); the discriminating variable is not fear level but friction and price point, and in 2 of the 4 successes the *paid standalone* revenue was subsequently absorbed into a platform bundle or given away free. Sub-class C (state resilience mandates): post-9/11 DHS, European defense post-2022, NERC CIP, pandemic stockpiles, fire codes, FDIC — 6 cases, 6 legislated within 2–6 years of the salient event, but 1 (pandemic stockpiles) was materially defunded within 4 years. [base-rate summary] Across 20 analogues: 19 of 20 exhibited the pattern in some form; median time from salient trigger to mainstream/mandated status ≈ 5–6 years (state mandates 2–6 years, enterprise compliance 3–6 years, household penetration 7–25 years); the failure modes are reversion after a date-certain threat passes, defunding once salience fades, and commoditization of the paid consumer layer by platform bundling.
reference_class.caveats: [caveat] Selection bias: security categories that became invisible infrastructure are easy to recall; the many micro-panics that produced no durable spend (bioterror home kits, EMP preparedness, most disaster-prep retail) are under-sampled, so the 19/20 hit rate overstates the unconditional base rate. [caveat] Composite resolution: the thesis requires 2 of 3 conditions, and the three sub-classes have very different base rates — (a) and (c) are high-probability given existing NIS2/DORA/CRA/CMMC/defense-floor legislation already in force, while (b) is the genuine binding constraint and historically the most likely to fail on the word 'paying'. Definitional drift in the survey instrument (counting bundled bank/telco/insurer protection vs standalone subscriptions) could flip (b) by 20+ points, so the metric is partly a measurement choice rather than a fact about the world. [caveat] Analogue non-independence: SOX, GDPR, AML, NIS2 and DORA are the same regulatory technology applied serially by an overlapping policy community — they are perhaps 2–3 independent observations, not 5. Likewise antivirus, identity monitoring and cyber insurance share the same underlying threat generator. [caveat] Denominator risk: the thesis is relative (security > convenience). In a nominal-5%-rates, high-inflation regime both numerator and denominator move; a convenience-spend collapse driven by a consumer recession could satisfy the relative claim without any security re-rating, and conversely AI-driven cost deflation in security tooling could cut vendor revenue growth while *protection intensity* rises — spend is an imperfect proxy for the behavioral shift. [caveat] Commoditization asymmetry: the historical record shows adoption and vendor economics decouple. Seatbelts, antivirus, credit monitoring and deposit insurance all reached universality while destroying or socializing the standalone profit pool. Investable exposure therefore depends on where the mandate lands in the value chain, not on whether the thesis resolves TRUE. [caveat] Trigger dependence: most analogues were detonated by a single vivid catastrophe. The 2026–2032 path is materially conditional on whether a mass-casualty cyber/infrastructure event or a NATO-adjacent kinetic escalation occurs; absent a trigger, the timeline skews to the slow end (10+ years) and (b) likely fails.

evidence.claim: Gartner/IDC vendor-side forecasts put global information-security end-user spending growth in the low-to-mid teens through 2026 (~$210-240B base), i.e. roughly 2-3x total IT spend growth — consistent with sub-condition (a).
evidence.source: Gartner / IDC security spending guides (vendor-survey methodology)

evidence.claim: CISO budget benchmarks (IANS/Artico) show average enterprise security budget growth decelerating to mid-single digits (4-8% y/y) since 2023 versus ~17% in 2022, and security's share of IT budget plateauing near 12-13% — directly threatens the '>10% CAGR with no year below +7%' floor.
evidence.source: IANS Research / Artico Search CISO Compensation & Budget Benchmark

evidence.claim: Binding resilience/cyber procurement law is already largely in force across OECD: EU NIS2 (transposition from Oct 2024), DORA (applied Jan 2025), Cyber Resilience Act (obligations from 2026-2027), UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, US CMMC phase-in from Nov 2025, Japan Active Cyber Defense law (2025) — sub-condition (c) is close to pre-satisfied.
evidence.source: EU Official Journal, DoD 48 CFR CMMC final rule, national statutes

evidence.claim: NATO's 2025 Hague commitment to 5% of GDP (3.5% core defense + 1.5% explicitly for resilience/critical infrastructure) creates a statutory-adjacent, multi-decade civil-preparedness procurement line in 20+ OECD states.
evidence.source: NATO Hague Summit declaration; EU ReArm/Readiness 2030

evidence.claim: Reported fraud losses keep compounding (FBI IC3 ~$16.6B in 2024, +33% y/y) and AI voice-cloning/deepfake scams are now mainstream press, raising threat salience — the loss-aversion trigger the mechanism depends on.
evidence.source: FBI IC3 annual report; FT reporting on AI-enabled scams

evidence.claim: A single cyberattack broke Boston Scientific's guidance (not demand), and enterprises (NVDA, PLTR, Booz Allen) restricted a frontier model vendor purely over data-handling fears — evidence that cyber risk is now a P&L and procurement gate, not an IT preference.

Mandatory reimbursement regimes (UK APP fraud reimbursement from Oct 2024, EU PSD3/PSR drafts, card-network zero-liability) shift fraud cost onto banks and issuers — making consumer protection free at point of use and structurally suppressing paid consumer security subscriptions, the core of sub-condition (b).
evidence.source: UK PSR policy statement; EU PSD3 file

evidence.claim: Historical precedent inside the same category: bundled free Microsoft Defender collapsed the paid consumer antivirus market, and breach-response credit monitoring is routinely given away for free after incidents — baseline protection commoditizes to zero price rather than becoming a majority paid subscription.
evidence.source: Gen Digital/NortonLifeLock consumer segment growth; AV market history

evidence.claim: US monitored-alarm penetration has hovered in the ~20-30% of households range for three decades despite repeated crime and disaster fear cycles; video doorbells scaled on convenience+one-time hardware, not on recurring monitoring subscriptions.

Current consumer attention data shows the fastest-rising query clusters are convenience/delegation (ai phone assistant, ai agent builder, cloud computing jobs) and entertainment (Netflix +10.3), with no consumer security cluster in the movers — the household leg of 'security beats convenience' is not visible in behavior today.

Security equities re-rate violently on threat headlines (CRWD/ZS +12%, PANW +11% on an AI-safety narrative day) and already carry high pricing scores (CRWD 89, PANW 84) — the market already treats cyber as non-discretionary, meaning the thesis is partly priced even if true.

Platform consolidation and agentic SOC automation are deflationary to unit pricing: vendors bundle point products free to win multi-year platform deals, and AI triage substitutes for analyst headcount — enterprise 'spend' can rise in seats/coverage while vendor revenue and budget dollars grow slower than 10%.
evidence.source: Vendor platformization disclosures (PANW, CRWD flex licensing)

evidence.claim: Private resilience procurement is already running ahead of statute on the energy side: Amazon's $8B generator order, Meta funding gas plants, Mitsui LNG contracted for data centers, Italy reversing its nuclear ban — firms are buying guaranteed electrons as a budgeted resilience line.

Cyber insurers now condition coverage and pricing on specific controls (MFA, EDR, immutable backups), and auditors/lenders increasingly require attestation — converting protection spend from optional to a condition of transacting.

Household budget stress is severe and worsening (7.45% mortgage rates, 65 months of above-target inflation, long-term unemployment third-highest since the GFC, visible consumer bifurcation), which historically causes churn in optional add-on subscriptions of exactly the identity/monitoring type.

Trust-shock fragility is demonstrated: vendor-side failures (SolarWinds, Okta, Change Healthcare, CrowdStrike's 2024 global outage) each re-priced the category and slowed consolidation — the mechanism's binding constraint (trusting a vendor with the keys) has already broken at least four times.

prerequisites_met: Threat salience is high and recurring (AI-enabled fraud, ransomware on hospitals/utilities, drone strikes on infrastructure, war proximity in Europe)
Regulatory scaffolding largely enacted: NIS2, DORA, CRA, CMMC, Japan ACD, NATO 5%/1.5% resilience line — sub-condition (c) effectively near-resolved
Insurance and audit gating makes controls a condition of transacting, not an option
Enterprise distribution mature: MSSP/MSP, cloud marketplaces, cyber insurers as channel
Switching costs already high in enterprise (agents, policy, audit continuity, multi-year ELAs)
Corporate energy-resilience procurement (behind-the-meter generation, firm capacity) is in visible dollar flow
prerequisites_missing: Consumer willingness to pay explicitly: paid identity/fraud/monitoring penetration is far below 50% in the US/EU and structurally undermined by free bundling and mandatory bank reimbursement
Sustained >10% enterprise cyber budget growth: CISO survey data currently shows mid-single-digit growth, contradicting vendor forecasts
A standardized, audited trust/certification regime for consumer security vendors (needed to survive the next vendor breach without category-wide churn)
Household-level resilience goods (backup power, stockpiles) are still event-driven, not budgeted recurring spend
Price discipline: platformization and agentic automation may raise coverage while deflating dollars
stage.historical_pathway_position: Between the Sarbanes-Oxley/PCI-DSS phase (mandate-driven enterprise compliance, already crossed) and the automotive-safety/deposit-insurance phase (protection fully embedded in the product, invisible and non-cancellable). Enterprise cyber sits at early majority on a SOX/EMV trajectory; consumer protection sits at innovators/early adopters on an antivirus-commoditization trajectory; state resilience procurement is at early majority on a post-9/11 DHS trajectory.

bull.description: A systemic, televised event — an AI-orchestrated fraud wave that empties retail accounts at scale, or a multi-day grid/cloud outage traced to state actors — makes protection legally compulsory and emotionally non-negotiable. All three sub-conditions resolve TRUE: enterprise cyber compounds >12% with a floor above 7% even in flat-IT years because it is carved out of IT budgets entirely and funded like insurance; bundled bank/telco/OEM 'protection lines' cross 50% adult penetration as explicitly priced line items (the EMV/airbag path); OECD statutes multiply past five into stockpile and firm-capacity mandates. Security vendors gain pricing power, defense and firm-power backlogs extend past 2035, and convenience/entertainment spend loses share outright in a high-rate, low-real-income regime.

base.description: The composite resolves TRUE on (c) plus a contested (a). Resilience statutes are already in force in well over five OECD states and expand; enterprise cyber grows high-single to low-double digits — comfortably faster than total IT but with at least one sub-7% year during the 2027-2029 cost-of-capital squeeze, making (a) a judgment call between vendor-revenue and CISO-budget measurement. Sub-condition (b) FAILS: consumer protection is absorbed into banks, card networks, telcos and device OEMs as a free or invisible feature rather than a majority-paid subscription, exactly as antivirus and credit monitoring were. Net: the thesis is directionally right and economically real, but the value accrues to distributors and compliance-gated incumbents, not to standalone consumer security brands — and much of the enterprise leg is already priced (CRWD 89, PANW 84).

bear.description: Security follows the antivirus/commoditization path on both legs. Agentic AI defense collapses the cost of adequate protection; hyperscalers and platform vendors bundle baseline security to zero marginal price; consolidation and 'good enough' free tiers cap budget growth at 5-7%, breaking sub-condition (a)'s floor. Mandatory reimbursement regimes make consumer fraud protection a bank liability, killing (b) outright. A 2027-2029 fiscal/consumer recession forces resilience mandates to be delayed or defunded (the post-COVID stockpile pattern: build, then quietly let it expire), and a major vendor trust shock — a second CrowdStrike-scale outage or an identity-provider breach — triggers category-wide churn and multiple compression. Only (c) holds; composite resolves FALSE, and the security trade turns out to have been a 2026 narrative hedge on AI capex rather than a durable wallet-share migration.

supporting: Cyber budget line items being moved out of IT budgets into risk/insurance or board-mandated reserves in 10-K/annual-report disclosure
Gartner/IDC security spend growth staying >2x total IT spend growth in a year when total IT grows <2% nominal — the explicit elasticity test
Bank, telco and card-issuer disclosures showing a separately priced 'protection' subscription ARPU line with >20% attach growth
New OECD statutes with procurement-linked enforcement: firm-capacity obligations, strategic stockpile mandates, or CRA-equivalents outside the EU
Defense and firm-power backlog extension (LMT/NOC/GD/LHX book-to-bill >1.2; GEV/VRT/ETN multi-year backlog coverage)
Cyber insurance attach rates and premium growth re-accelerating with control-conditioned underwriting
Enterprise on-prem/sovereign AI deployments growing faster than public-cloud AI inference, indicating security-driven architecture choices

second_order_thesis: The first-order trade (buy cybersecurity) is already the market's reflexive hedge on AI capex risk and is priced accordingly — CRWD at 89 and PANW at 84 on internal pricing scores are the theme being right and the entry being wrong. The second-order insight is that security will follow the seatbelt/airbag/EMV path, not the subscription path: protection wins by disappearing into products people already buy, which means the consumer leg of this thesis (sub-condition b) most likely fails as a measured survey outcome while the economics of it accrue entirely to distributors — card networks, issuers, telcos, device OEMs and banks — who capture a fraud-defense rent inside interchange and premium fees without ever selling a security product. Third-order: mandatory reimbursement and free bundling mean the marginal dollar of consumer resilience spend does not go to identity subscriptions at all, it goes to electrons and hard assets — the backup generator, the heat pump, the gold, the stay-put renovation — which is precisely where the attention data says the market has not marked it (LOW, HD, SHW, EOG all in the not-priced bucket). Fourth-order: agentic AI is the bidirectional wildcard. It industrializes fraud (inflationary to defense budgets) and it automates defense (deflationary to defense revenue), so enterprise security coverage can expand while vendor dollars compress — meaning the durable exposure is not the software vendor but the compliance gate (attestation, ratings, insurance) and the physical chokepoint (firm capacity, switchgear, munitions, skilled trades) whose supply cannot be automated away. The single highest-asymmetry expression of this thesis is therefore NOT cyber software; it is contracted-backlog owners of resilience hardware and power, bought while the narrative score (power demand 85, grid 77) runs 40+ points ahead of the pricing score (34, 55).

source_bullets.text: Security is replacing convenience as the dominant consumer and corporate need — energy security, supply-chain security, cyber security (a single cyberattack broke Boston Scientific's guidance, not demand).

Security 
physical, energy, and digital 
is replacing convenience as the premium people and institutions will pay for. Cybersecurity budgets become non-discretionary as AI supercharges scams (FT: criminals using AI for scams), and energy security drives national LNG/nuclear procurement.

Security — physical, energy and digital — becomes a standing consumption category: Italy restarting nuclear, a drone strike on a UAE nuclear plant, Danish intelligence warning Russia could hit NATO within months, exchange hacks. Households and states both spend on resilience ahead of optimisation.
